title: 6 Functions, 6 Rules, 6 Theorems
6 Functions, 6 Rules, 6 Theorems
6 Functions, 6 Rules, 6 Theorems
text:
Six theorems









Item and key formula
Example
Application




1. Fundamental TheoremIf f(x) = \int_a^x s(t)\,dt then f' = s;\int_a^b f'(x)\,dx = f(b) - f(a)
\int_0^3 2x\,dx = 3^2 - 0^2 = \mathbf{9} (no Riemann sums)\tfrac{d}{dx}\int_0^x \cos t\,dt = \mathbf{\cos x}
Velocity → distance; flow rate → total volume; demand rate → cumulative demand; PDF → CDF


2. Max–min / intermediate valueContinuous f on [a, b] reaches a max and a min, and every value between
x^2 on [-1, 2]: max \mathbf{4} at x = 2, min \mathbf{0} at x = 0Counterexample: the step on [-1, 1] never equals 0.5 (not continuous)
Guarantees an optimum exists (basis of optimization); justifies bisection root-finding


3. Mean Valuef'(c) = \tfrac{f(b) - f(a)}{b - a} for some c in (a, b)
x^2 on [0, 2]: average slope = 4/2 = 2; f'(c) = 2c = 2 \to \mathbf{c = 1}Drive 120 km in 2 h → at some instant exactly 60 km/h
Average-speed cameras; proving error bounds for numerical methods


4. Taylor seriesf(x) = f(a) + f'(a)(x-a) + \tfrac{f''(a)}{2!}(x-a)^2 + \dots
e^x \approx 1 + x + \tfrac{x^2}{2} \to at x = 0.1: \mathbf{1.105} (true 1.10517)\sin x \approx x - \tfrac{x^3}{6}
How calculators compute \sin, e^x, \sqrt{\phantom{x}}; \sin\theta \approx \theta for pendulums; gradient descent / Newton’s method


5. Taylor remainderCut after x^2: error = \tfrac{f'''(c)}{3!}(x-a)^3, c between a and x
e^x at x = 0.1: error = \tfrac{e^c}{6}\cdot 0.001, between 0.000167 and 0.000184Actual error 0.000171 ✓
Knowing how accurate an approximation is; choosing step size or number of terms in solvers


6. Binomial(1+x)^p = 1 + px + \tfrac{p(p-1)}{2!}x^2 + \dots
p = 2: 1 + 2x + x^2 (stops)p = \tfrac12: \sqrt{1.1} \approx 1 + 0.05 - 0.00125 = \mathbf{1.04875} (true 1.04881)p = -1: 1 - x + x^2 - \dots (never stops)
Quick approximations, e.g. (1+r)^n \approx 1 + nr; relativity \gamma \approx 1 + \tfrac{v^2}{2c^2}; binomial distribution

title: 6 Functions, 6 Rules, 6 Theorems
text:
The big picture
The functions describe how things behave (growth, cycles, switches); the rules let you differentiate complex models built from those pieces; the theorems guarantee that optimization and approximation actually work.

title: Linear Regression and Gradient Descent
text: Full lecture: CS229 Lecture 2 on YouTube (Stanford has disabled embedding, so it opens on YouTube). The video above is a shorter companion on the same idea.

title: Linear Regression and Gradient Descent
text:
Key ideas
A linear hypothesis with x_0 = 1 for the intercept:

h_\theta(x) = \sum_{j=0}^{d} \theta_j x_j = \theta^\top x

The least-squares cost over n training examples:

J(\theta) = \frac{1}{2} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \left( h_\theta(x^{(i)}) - y^{(i)} \right)^2

title: Linear Regression and Gradient Descent
text:
Gradient descent
Repeat until convergence, for every j at once:

\theta_j := \theta_j - \alpha \sum_{i=1}^{n} \left( h_\theta(x^{(i)}) - y^{(i)} \right) x_j^{(i)}


Batch gradient descent uses all n examples per step: an exact gradient, but slow on large data.
Stochastic gradient descent updates after each example: noisy, but it starts making progress immediately.







TipLearning rate



If J(\theta) goes up between iterations, \alpha is too large. Try dividing it by about 3 each time.


import numpy as np

def batch_gradient_descent(X, y, alpha=0.01, iters=1000):
    """X: (n, d+1) with a leading column of ones; y: (n,)."""
    theta = np.zeros(X.shape[1])
    for _ in range(iters):
        residual = X @ theta - y
        theta -= alpha * X.T @ residual / len(y)
    return theta

title: Linear Regression and Gradient Descent
text:
Normal equations
Setting \nabla_\theta J(\theta) = 0 gives a closed form:

\theta = (X^\top X)^{-1} X^\top y

theta = np.linalg.solve(X.T @ X, X.T @ y)  # more stable than an explicit inverse
